source.title: Anatomy of Unlearning: The Dual Impact of Fact Salience and Model Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Anna Borisiuk; Andrey Savchenko; Alexander Panchenko; Elena Tutubalina

page_placements.theme: Internal analyses: changes concentrated late or along a direction, target representations stay close to the original

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some tables and formulas are flattened in the text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: It tests how unlearning methods affect targeted factual performance and general capability, but does not test post-unlearning recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates GA, GD, NPO and UNDIAL unlearning on factual QA. It does not fine-tune unlearned models on recovery data, ablate directions, quantize weights, or test prompt-based recovery. Its representation analyses do not test whether an edit restores knowledge or establish that unlearning merely blocks access. Cited results about benign relearning are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study measures how far GA, GD and NPO unlearning (UNDIAL in an appendix) lower forget-set QA performance on real Wikidata facts. It also checks task retain-set and general capability (MMLU, HellaSwag). This bears on the efficacy and capability parts of version A in a new setting: fact popularity, and pretrained vs SFT models. No recovery attack of any kind is run, so B–F and A's attack-resistance part are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that unlearning outcomes depend jointly on fact popularity and training stage. Pretrained models are unstable and prone to abrupt degradation, and show apparent relearning of popular facts (ROUGE-based). SFT models forget more smoothly, with 10–50% higher retention at the same learning rate, though forgetting popular facts in SFT models hurts the retain set more. General capability (MMLU, HellaSwag) stays within 3%. No recovery attacks are tested.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates GA, GD, NPO, and UNDIAL on DUET fact QA and compares pretrained with SFT models; it does not reproduce the recovery methods in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with model training stage, fact popularity, learning rate, epoch count, and forget-set size. The text says one epoch yields insufficient forgetting, three epochs cause excessive degradation, and learning rates above 5 × 10−5 cause catastrophic forgetting while rates below 10−6 yield negligible unlearning.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix B.5, Tables 6–7: in pretrained models, hidden states for unlearned facts stay highly similar to the base model (mean cosine 0.981–0.996; SFT 0.958–0.973). Gold-answer rank for popular facts barely moves (Δrank 7.5 GA, 1.1 NPO), while rare facts under pretrained GA move from rank about 9 to about 230. The authors read this as limited internal adaptation in pretrained models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-based unlearning of pretrained LLMs leaves internal representations of the targeted facts largely unchanged, consistent with shallow modification. This is not tested by any recovery attack.

record.problems: The main experiment focuses on LLaMA-3.1-8B and a city-domain forget set with a compact retain set. The authors identify the popularity labels as proxies and note that broader domains and larger models remain future work. The reported QA metrics are not chance-level accuracy measures; general-capability results are summarized as within 3% and displayed in a figure. No recovery-attack evaluation or uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also reports judge fluency, other learning rates and epochs, N = 1% and 10%, UNDIAL, full-parameter SFT comparisons, and appendix experiments for Gemma, Qwen, and multi-domain data. These were not extracted because the main rows already capture the tested target-performance and capability outcomes; no recovery attacks are reported in those additional experiments either.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks (relearning, prompting, quantization, ablation) recover the unlearned facts.
All; no direction ablation. The hidden-state analysis does not test blocking vs deletion.
All; no rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery.
All; no robustness-claiming method evaluated against attacks.

missing.what: LLM-judge Accuracy on the task retain set for all 12 unlearned LLaMA configurations. SFT-popular falls 0.862 to 0.555 (GA), 0.588 (GD) and 0.683 (NPO). Pretrained-rare GA falls 0.839 to 0.670; the others fall 0.01–0.09. rows_left_out names judge fluency but not this column. It corroborates the retain-cost rows R13–R24.

record.verdict_notes: Changes from the earlier verdict: (1) The five grouped row_fixes items were split into one item per row (R01–R38), each changing V1 to A, as the merge requires. States are unchanged. (2) R17 and R19–R21 moved out of the supports label and into limits_scope. Their retain sets are near-unchanged only because forgetting in the same configurations was weak (R05, corrected to 0.756) or reversed (R07–R09), so they do not show capability kept while forgetting. Supports now rests on R37–R38 only. (3) R13–R16 and R18 (retain drops of 0.05–0.15) were added to limits_scope, and the epoch note was added to the challenges reason. (4) The earlier missing entry, with versions "none (fits_no_version)", was removed. That is not a declared identifier, and the result bears on no version. The finding stays in fits_no_version, now with its locator and numbers. (5) A missing entry was added for Judge Accuracy on the retain set (Table 1), which rows_left_out does not declare. Kept from before: R05's value was misread from Table 1. The ROUGE 'relearning' in pretrained-popular models is not matched by Judge Accuracy, which falls slightly. All main results come from one chosen lr (2e-5) and epoch count (2), picked by the authors as a compromise. Context from results declared left out: Gemma-7B (Table 5) does not show the pretrained-popular rise. Its pretrained-popular forget ROUGE falls to 0.03–0.43, and SFT GA popular reaches 0.000 at a retain cost of −0.61. So the challenges label is specific to LLaMA, and its condition already says so. Gemma, Qwen, multi-domain, UNDIAL, other learning rates, N=1%/10% and full-parameter SFT results were declared left out. No instructions were found in the study text.

versions.untested_parts: It measures targeted-answer performance after unlearning and general benchmark capability, but does not test whether attacks recover knowledge.
No activation-direction ablation or test of restored knowledge; the internal representation analyses do not establish blocking rather than deletion.
No prompt-rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context recovery experiment.
No evaluation of a method claiming resistance to recovery attacks.

relationships.condition: Pretrained LLaMA-3.1-8B, popular forget set, GA/GD/NPO, N=5%, lr=2e-5
relationships.reason: Forget ROUGE-L rises from 0.766 to 0.91–0.92 (R07–R09); the authors report the rise at all epochs 1–3. Judge accuracy drops only 0.10–0.12, to about 0.80 (R31, R33, R35), far from chance.
relationships.display_finding: Forget ROUGE-L rose from 0.766 to 0.91–0.92 across epochs 1–3, while judge accuracy decreased only 0.10–0.12 to approximately 0.80.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: Pretrained LLaMA-3.1-8B, popular forget set, GA/GD/NPO, N=5%, lr=2e-5
source_check.reason: Forget ROUGE-L rises from 0.766 to 0.908-0.922 and judge accuracy stays at about 0.79-0.82 (baseline 0.915). The authors say explicitly that the model improves on the forget set at epochs 1-3, so the effect is reversed.

relationships.condition: Pretrained-rare and SFT rare/popular forgetting (GA/GD/NPO, N=5%, lr=2e-5), plus the task retain set in all eight settings
relationships.reason: Forget measures drop but stay well above zero (ROUGE 0.21–0.76, judge acc 0.25–0.57; R01–R06, R10–R12, R25–R30, R32, R34, R36). Retain ROUGE falls 0.14–0.26 for SFT-popular (R22–R24), 0.08–0.15 for pretrained-rare (R13–R15) and 0.05–0.06 for SFT-rare GA/NPO (R16, R18). It stays intact mainly where forgetting was weak or reversed (R17 with R05; R19–R21 with R07–R09). The authors report that higher lr causes catastrophic forgetting.
relationships.display_finding: Forget ROUGE remained 0.21–0.76 and judge accuracy 0.25–0.57, while retain ROUGE fell 0.14–0.26 for SFT-popular, 0.08–0.15 for pretrained-rare, and 0.05–0.06 for SFT-rare GA/NPO; retention mainly held where forgetting was weak or reversed, and higher learning rates caused catastrophic forgetting.
